notes.summary: In Error Spotting a sentence is split into three parts and a fourth option says No error. Find the part with the grammar mistake. SSC asks 2–3 such questions in Tier 1 and 3–4 in Tier 2, and nearly all of them test a small set of fixed rules.

concepts.title: Read the whole sentence first
concepts.body:
Do not judge each part alone. Read the full sentence, find the real subject and its main verb, then check the small words.
  1. Subject and verb: singular or plural?
  2. Tense: does it match the time words (yesterday, since, by next year)?
  3. Articles, prepositions and pronouns.
  4. Fixed pairs: no sooner…than, hardly…when, not only…but also.

concepts.title: Subject–verb agreement
concepts.body:
The verb agrees with the real subject, not with the nearest noun.
  • The quality of the mangoes is good. (subject = quality)
  • Words joined by as well as, along with, together with do not change the subject: The teacher, along with his students, was present.
  • Each, every, either, neither, everyone take a singular verb.

concepts.title: Tense and time words
concepts.body:
• Since / for with a period up to now → present perfect: I have lived here since 2015.
  • A past time word (yesterday, last year, in 2010) → simple past, never present perfect.
  • After if in a future condition, use simple present: If it rains, we will stay in.

concepts.title: Pronouns and comparison
concepts.body: After than / as, the pronoun case follows the hidden verb: He is taller than I (am). After prepositions use the object form: between you and me. In comparisons compare like with like: The climate of Shimla is better than that of Delhi.

varieties.name: Subject–verb agreement
varieties.how: Find the true subject (skip phrases with of, along with, as well as) and match the verb to it.

example.q: (A) One of my friends / (B) have gone / (C) to Canada for studies. / (D) No error
steps: Real subject is One, which is singular.

varieties.name: Tense errors
varieties.how: Look for time words. Since/for → perfect tense; a fixed past time → simple past; if-clause about future → simple present.

example.q: (A) I have seen / (B) that film / (C) last Sunday. / (D) No error
steps: last Sunday is a fixed past time.

varieties.name: Pronouns, prepositions and comparison
varieties.how: Check pronoun case after prepositions and than; check fixed prepositions (superior to, prefer to, married to); compare like with like.

example.q: (A) This matter is / (B) strictly between / (C) you and I. / (D) No error
steps: between is a preposition, so it needs the object form.

tips: Always locate the subject–verb pair first; it is the most tested rule.
Mark 'No error' only after you have checked articles, prepositions and tense; SSC does use it as the correct answer sometimes.
Words like superior, inferior, senior, junior, prefer take to, not than.
traps: The noun closest to the verb is often a decoy: in The box of pencils is… the verb follows box, not pencils.
Hardly and scarcely pair with when, but no sooner pairs with than.

questions.q:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error.
The list of selected candidates / have been put up / on the notice board.
questions.solution: The subject is list (singular); of selected candidates only describes it. So the verb should be has been put up.

questions.q:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error.
My uncle has visited us / last month and stayed / for a week.
questions.solution: last month is a fixed point in the past, so the simple past is needed: My uncle visited us. Present perfect cannot be used with a definite past time.

questions.q:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error.
The manager, as well as his assistants, / were present / at the annual meeting.
options: The manager, as well as his assistants,
questions.solution: When two nouns are joined by as well as, the verb agrees with the first noun. The manager is singular, so use was present.

questions.q:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error.
Many people believe that / village life is superior / than city life.
questions.solution: Superior is a Latin comparative and takes to, not than: superior to city life.

questions.q:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error.
No sooner had the bell rung / when the children rushed / out of their classrooms.
options: No sooner had the bell rung
questions.solution: No sooner is always followed by than, not when: than the children rushed. (Hardly/Scarcely take when.)

questions.q:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error.
The population of Mumbai / is larger than / any other city in India.
questions.solution: We must compare population with population, not population with a city. Correct: that of any other city in India.
